unit_label: Module C unit 4 (courseware unit 20): term loans, deferred payment guarantees, project appraisal, commercial appraisal ratios, project and infrastructure finance, partial credit enhancement

facts.statement: Banks normally provide term loans for acquiring fixed assets such as land, buildings, plant and machinery and infrastructure, and for personal consumption, educational and similar loans, while working capital loans sustain current assets. In exceptional cases banks give term loans for current assets, called Working Capital Term Loans (WCTL), when the enterprise cannot bring in the NWC needed for the desired current ratio from its long-term sources and would otherwise face a liquidity crunch. Working capital loans are normally sanctioned for one year and are payable on demand, while term loans are repayable on an agreed schedule stipulated in the sanction terms, so term loans are treated as long-term assets and working capital loans as short-term assets for matching the bank's assets and liabilities; a working capital loan is in practice continued while the working is satisfactory. Because a term loan is repaid out of future cash flows, the DSCR matters most in its appraisal, while liquidity ratios matter most for working capital loans.

There is no uniform repayment schedule for term loans: each loan has its own schedule depending on the cash surplus of the borrower. A salaried person may repay by EMI; a farmer's principal and interest may coincide with the cropping pattern; for industrial enterprises banks normally stipulate monthly or quarterly repayment of principal; in some cases the entire amount with accumulated interest may be stipulated in one instalment, called bullet repayment.

A Deferred Payment Guarantee (DPG) is issued by the bank when the purchaser of a fixed asset does not pay the supplier immediately but pays according to an agreed repayment schedule, and the bank guarantees the repayment; it is a non-fund based method of financing purchase of fixed assets. If the purchaser defaults in payment of any amount, the bank has to pay the supplier and the exposure becomes fund based until recovered from the client. The risks in a DPG are the same as in a term loan, so the appraisal of a DPG is the same as for a term loan.

Standalone term loan appraisal need not apply every concept of project appraisal, though all concepts of project appraisal apply to project finance. In project finance all financial needs of the enterprise, including working capital, are appraised, because the total requirement of long-term funds includes margin money for working capital; after assessing the total long-term requirement the bank decides the amount to be sanctioned and the contribution of the promoters. For an existing enterprise buying machinery without a major change in the volume or composition of business, a detailed examination of techno-economic feasibility, managerial competence and IRR is of little use; examining projections for the next two to three years to check that the DSCR is satisfactory is enough, and for individual loans such as housing and education loans the projected DSCR may be enough to judge viability. The basic principles of appraisal of a project or a standalone term loan are not different.

Project appraisal covers eight areas: prima facie acceptability, management, environmental, economic, market, technical, financial and commercial appraisal. Prima facie acceptability checks that the proposed industry, activity and exposure comply with the law of the land, fit regulatory prescriptions of RBI, are acceptable under the bank's loan policy and fair banking risk management advisory. Management appraisal examines the persons behind the enterprise (owners and key managerial personnel), since confidence is the basis of all credit transactions, based on the five Cs of the borrower: character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions, plus reliability, responsibility and resources; pre-sanction steps include interviewing the borrower, pre-sanction inspection or survey and compliance with Know Your Customer norms. Environmental appraisal covers the impact of the environment on the project and of the project on the environment (water, air, land, sound, geographical location, clearances from the pollution control board, permission and licences). Economic appraisal examines whether the incremental production will be accepted by the wider economy and whether the growth pattern of the economy is up or flattening. Market appraisal, a subset of economic appraisal, is a demand-supply gap analysis covering whether the market can absorb the incremental production, entry of competitors, headroom to grow, import substitution, past trends, end use, prospects and feasibility of export.

Technical appraisal studies availability of basic infrastructure, licensing and registration requirements, selection of technology and suitable technical process, availability of raw material and skilled and unskilled labour, offtake of products, technology used in the production process and product, and whether the overall technological background is sunrise, stable or sunset. Financial appraisal studies analysis of past working results in the case of existing concerns, determination of the cost of the project, assessment of the sources of funds and uses of funds, balance sheet and ratio analysis, profitability estimates, and funds flow and cash flow projections. The items of cost of the project (CoP) are land and site development, building and other civil works, plant and machinery, furniture, fixtures and fittings, vehicles and equipment, preliminary and pre-operative expenses, interest during construction, contingencies and working capital margin; the means of finance (MoF) are share capital (existing and infusion), reserves and surplus, internal accruals during construction, capital subsidy, unsecured loans from promoters, friends and relatives, term loans, deferred payment guarantee and subordinated debts. A cushion should be provided in costs for inflationary increase during implementation, and the sources must be identified to meet the cost.

Estimates of cost of production and profitability are needed to see whether the unit can make the products at costs yielding a sufficient margin in a competitive market, because repayment capacity is linked to the ability to generate surplus. Profitability is estimated over the project period or the proposed repayment period of the loan, whichever is longer, and estimates rest on installed capacity, the number of shifts per day and working days, capacity build-up and utilisation, product mix, labour and other direct costs, the quantity and price of input and output, and unit cost of production.

Commercial appraisal measures the business's capability to generate enough profit to service its debts in relation to time and quantity, from two perspectives: ability of repayment and cushion to fall back if unpaid. The break even point (BEP) is the point at which total cost equals sales revenue. Fixed cost does not change with the level of production in the installed capacity (for example depreciation); variable cost varies in proportion to output (for example raw material); total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Contribution is selling price per unit less variable cost per unit, because it contributes first towards recovery of fixed cost and then generates profit. Break even point in units = fixed cost / contribution per unit; as a share of installed capacity it is that number divided by capacity; the margin of safety is 1 minus the break even point (as a share of capacity) when actual capacity utilisation is full, that is the share of capacity beyond break even. For example, with installed capacity of 1,000 units a year, fixed cost Rs 2,000, variable cost Rs 7 per unit and selling price Rs 12, contribution is Rs 5, break even is 400 units or 40 per cent of capacity, and from the 401st unit the unit generates profit. If the volume data are not available, break even sales volume = fixed cost / (total sales revenue - total variable cost) x total sales revenue at that level of capacity utilisation. The break even point also determines the moratorium period required and the time from which repayment can commence. As a rule of thumb the courseware gives break even of up to 50 per cent of capacity as very healthy, with higher levels progressively riskier and above 85 per cent very high risk.

The Debt Service Coverage Ratio decides the ideal amount of repayment instalments in each year so that debt servicing is strainless; the courseware considers a gross DSCR of 1.50 to 1.75 and a net DSCR of about 2 ideal. Net DSCR = cash accrual / instalments of term loans due in the period; gross DSCR = (cash accrual + interest on term loans) / (instalments + interest on term loans). The average DSCR for the entire repayment period is not the arithmetic mean of the yearly ratios but the horizontal sum of cash accruals plus interest on all term loans for all the years divided by the horizontal sum of term loan instalments due plus interest on all term loans for the corresponding period (interest being included in numerator and denominator only for the average gross DSCR).

The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes the net present value of all future cash flows from the investment equal to zero in a discounted cash flow analysis; it is a look-out of the investor to know what rate of return she gets, and lenders use it to judge whether the project would interest the investor and so whether recovery is likely; it is also called the Discounted Cash Flow Rate of Return or the rate of return. Sensitivity analysis recognises that projections rest on assumptions that may fail: it shows the impact on BEP, DSCR and IRR of adverse change in any input or output price. Normally four adverse scenarios are examined individually (the most sensitive areas) against the base scenario, and a fifth scenario in which all four adverse changes occur together; the banker proceeds only if BEP, DSCR and IRR remain at acceptable levels. The Fixed Asset Coverage Ratio (written down value of fixed assets under charge over term loans outstanding) and the Security Margin Coverage Ratio ((WDV of fixed assets - term loans outstanding) / WDV of fixed assets x 100) assess the security cushion.

Infrastructure projects have exceptionally long implementation, gestation and pay back periods and a high debt-equity ratio; this long-term deployment reduces the risk for the lender in the sense that its funds are assured of deployment for a long time. The basic principles of appraisal are the same as for any project but additional points are considered. Infrastructure sectors, as the courseware lists them from the Gazette, fall under five heads: transport (roads, bridges, ports, airports, railway track), energy (electricity generation, transmission, distribution, oil and gas pipelines), water and sanitation, communication (telecommunication) and social and commercial infrastructure (education institutions, hospitals, certain hotels, common infrastructure for industrial parks, agriculture infrastructure and so on).

A bank finances technically feasible, financially viable and bankable infrastructure projects of public and private sector undertakings if it has the expertise to appraise technical feasibility, financial viability and bankability (with risk analysis and sensitivity analysis); term loans to public sector units are sanctioned only to corporate entities (companies or statutory corporations), must not substitute budgetary resources and must not finance State budgets; the revenue stream of the project must be sufficient to service the debt, not budgetary resources; funding proposals for SPVs must be for specific monitorable projects; and private sector SPVs must directly undertake financially viable infrastructure projects, not act as mere financial intermediaries, with the bank ensuring that the parent or sponsor's financial difficulty does not affect the SPV. Credit facilities may be working capital finance, term loan, project loan and subscription to bonds, debentures, preference shares or equity shares acquired as part of the project finance package (treated as deemed advance), and any other funded or non-funded facility. For infrastructure projects of Government-owned entities the bank does diligence on viability and State Government guarantees are not a substitute for credit appraisal. Because infrastructure projects are often financed through SPVs, the bank evaluates project risks, risk mitigation through project contracts and creditworthiness of the contracting entities, and may constitute screening committees or special cells; where the funding need is large, participating banks may rely on the lead bank's appraisal report under consortium or syndication. Prudential exposure limits, risk weights and asset-liability management apply (the bank watches liquidity mismatches from long-term lending), and the bank sets a clear approval procedure and a mechanism to review applications pending beyond the specified period, avoiding multiplicity of appraisals.

Under the Project Finance chapter (effective 1 October 2025; not applicable to projects whose financial closure was achieved by that date) a project has three phases: design (genesis to financial closure), construction (financial closure to the day before the actual date of commencement of commercial operations, DCCO) and operational (from the actual DCCO until full repayment). Before disbursement the bank ensures financial closure is achieved and the original DCCO is documented, the project-specific disbursement schedule linked to stage of completion is in the loan agreement, and the post-DCCO repayment schedule is realistic, with the original or revised repayment tenor including moratorium not more than 85 per cent of the economic life of the project. The DCCO is the same across all lenders. In under-construction projects where aggregate exposure of lenders is up to Rs 1,500 crore no individual bank may hold less than 10 per cent of aggregate exposure; where it is more than Rs 1,500 crore, an individual bank's floor is 5 per cent or Rs 150 crore, whichever is higher; the floors do not apply after actual DCCO. All applicable approvals and clearances (environmental, legal, regulatory) are obtained before financial closure. Before disbursement the bank ensures minimum land or right of way: 50 per cent for infrastructure projects under the PPP model, 75 per cent for all other projects, and as the bank decides for transmission line projects. For PPP infrastructure projects disbursement begins only after the Appointed Date is declared. Disbursal is proportionate to stages of completion, equity infusion and other sources, and the lender's independent engineer or architect certifies the stages. A project finance account may be classified as NPA before actual DCCO according to the record of recovery. The bank keeps a project-specific database and updates changes within 15 days.

A bank may provide Partial Credit Enhancement (PCE) to bonds issued by corporates or special purpose vehicles for funding all types of projects and to bonds of non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size of Rs 1,000 crore and above registered with RBI (including HFCs), to improve the rating of the bonds so that issuers can raise funds on better terms. PCE is a subordinated facility in the form of an irrevocable contingent line of credit drawn if there is a shortfall in cash flows for servicing the bonds, and may be made available as a revolving facility. The exposure of a single bank by way of PCE is 50 per cent of the bond issue size, and the aggregate PCE exposure of all providers for a bond issue is also capped at 50 per cent. PCE is provided at the time of the bond issue, is irrevocable and cannot be provided by way of guarantee. A bank may offer PCE only for bonds whose pre-enhanced rating is not lower than BBB minus from accredited external credit assessment institutions, the bonds must be rated by a minimum of two ECAIs at all times, and the rating reports disclose both the standalone rating and the enhanced rating. A bank does not invest in corporate bonds credit-enhanced by any regulated entity but may give other need-based credit facilities to the issuer. A clear legally binding agreement documents the arrangement among the promoter, the PCE-providing bank, the bondholders (through the trustee) and all other lenders.

Take-out financing is a mechanism by which a bank financing a long-tenor infrastructure loan arranges for another financial institution to take over the outstanding loan on a pre-determined basis, to avoid asset-liability maturity mismatches. The RBI statement is that loan transfers must transfer economic interest without any change to the loan terms, and if terms are modified during or after a transfer (for example in take-out financing) the modification is evaluated against restructuring under the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025.

payload.title: Term loans and how they differ from working capital loans
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Term loans** fund **fixed assets** (land, buildings, plant, machinery, infrastructure) and personal, consumption and education needs. **Working capital loans** fund **current assets**.

| | **Term loan** | **Working capital loan** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Repayment** | **Agreed schedule** in the sanction terms | Normally sanctioned for **one year**, **payable on demand** (renewed while working is satisfactory) |
| **Bank's asset–liability matching** | **Long-term asset** | **Short-term asset** |
| **Repaid from** | **Future cash flows** | Operating cycle |
| **Key ratio** | **DSCR** | **Liquidity ratios** |

**WCTL (working capital term loan):** exceptionally, a **term loan for current assets** when the firm cannot bring in the **NWC** needed for the desired **current ratio** from long-term sources and would face a **liquidity crunch**.

**Repayment patterns:** no uniform schedule. **EMI** for a salaried person; **cropping pattern** for a farmer; **monthly or quarterly principal** for industrial units; **bullet** repayment of principal and interest in one instalment in some cases.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The repayment schedule is set from the borrower's cash surplus, not from a fixed formula.

self_check.prompt_text: Which ratio matters most in appraising a term loan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The DSCR, because the loan is repaid from future cash flows.

payload.title: Deferred payment guarantees (DPGs)
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **DPG** is a **bank guarantee** given when a buyer of a **fixed asset** pays the supplier **in instalments** instead of at once. The bank guarantees the instalments.

- It is a **non-fund based** way of financing the purchase of fixed assets.
- If the buyer **defaults**, the bank **pays the supplier** and the exposure becomes **fund based** until recovered.
- The **risks are the same as in a term loan**, so a DPG is **appraised like a term loan**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: DPG also appears as a source of finance for a project.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to a DPG exposure if the buyer defaults?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The bank pays the supplier and the exposure turns fund based until it recovers from the client.

payload.title: Term loan appraisal versus project appraisal
payload.core_explanation_md:
| | **Project appraisal** | **Standalone term loan appraisal** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | **All financial needs** including **working capital margin**; the bank decides the **total long-term funds**, the **loan** and the **promoters' contribution** | Only the **loan** for the asset |
| For an existing firm buying machinery without major change | | A detailed **techno-economic**, **management** and **IRR** study is of little use; check **projected DSCR for 2-3 years** |
| For housing or education loans | | **Projected DSCR** may suffice |

The **basic principles are the same**; the standalone appraisal is simply **simpler**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Project appraisal is the full set of eight areas on the next card.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does project appraisal include working capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the total long-term funds needed include the margin money for working capital.

payload.title: The eight areas of project appraisal: acceptability, management, environment, economy, market
payload.core_explanation_md:
The eight areas: **prima facie acceptability, management, environmental, economic, market, technical, financial and commercial** appraisal.

| Area | The question |
| --- | --- |
| **Prima facie acceptability** | Is the activity **legal**, within **RBI prescriptions**, the **bank's loan policy** and **fair risk management**? |
| **Management** | Who are the **owners and key managers**? The **5 Cs**: **character, capacity, capital, collateral, conditions**, plus reliability, responsibility and resources. Pre-sanction: **interview**, **inspection or survey**, **KYC** |
| **Environmental** | Effect of the **environment on the project** and of the **project on the environment**: water, air, land, sound, location, **pollution control board clearance**, licences |
| **Economic** | Will the **wider economy** absorb the **incremental production**? Is growth **up or flattening**? |
| **Market** (a **subset of economic**) | **Demand-supply gap**, **competitors**, **headroom to grow**, **import substitution**, trends, end use, **export** feasibility |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Confidence in the people behind the project is the basis of all credit transactions.

self_check.prompt_text: Which appraisal area is a subset of economic appraisal?

payload.title: Technical and financial appraisal, cost of the project and means of finance
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Technical appraisal:** **infrastructure** availability, **licences**, **technology and process**, **raw material and labour**, **offtake** of products, and whether the technology is **sunrise, stable or sunset**.

**Financial appraisal:** **past results** (existing concerns), **cost of the project**, **sources and uses of funds**, **balance sheet and ratios**, **profitability estimates**, **funds flow and cash flow** projections.

| **Cost of the project (CoP)** | **Means of finance (MoF)** |
| --- | --- |
| Land and site development | Share capital (existing and new) |
| Building and civil works | Reserves and surplus |
| Plant and machinery | Internal accruals during construction |
| Furniture, fixtures, fittings | Capital subsidy |
| Vehicles and equipment | **Unsecured loans** from promoters, friends, relatives |
| Preliminary and pre-operative expenses | **Term loans** |
| **Interest during construction** | **Deferred payment guarantee** |
| **Contingencies** | **Subordinated debts** |
| **Working capital margin** | |

**Provide a cushion** in the cost for **inflation** during implementation. **Profitability estimates** run over the project period or the repayment period, **whichever is longer**, using **capacity, shifts, utilisation, product mix, input and output prices, labour and direct costs**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: CoP must equal MoF: every rupee of cost needs an identified source.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two items of cost of the project that are not physical assets.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest during construction and contingencies (also preliminary and pre-operative expenses and working capital margin).

payload.title: Matching cost of the project with the means of finance
payload.core_explanation_md: A project has these costs (Rs lakh): land and site development 20, building 60, plant and machinery 200, furniture and vehicles 20, preliminary expenses 10, interest during construction 30, contingencies 10 and working capital margin 30. The means of finance are share capital 100, internal accruals 20, unsecured loans from promoters 30, capital subsidy 20 and a term loan. Find the total cost, the term loan needed and the debt equity ratio on share capital.

worked_steps.description: Total cost of the project.
Means of finance other than the term loan.
Term loan = total cost - other means.
Debt equity ratio on share capital.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Total cost Rs 380 lakh; term loan Rs 210 lakh; debt equity ratio 2.10 : 1 on share capital

self_check.prompt_text: If the capital subsidy were not received, what would the term loan have to be?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 230 lakh, since the cost is fixed and every source must add to Rs 380 lakh.

payload.title: Commercial appraisal: break even analysis
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Commercial appraisal** tests **ability of repayment** and the **cushion if unpaid**.

**Break even point (BEP):** total cost = sales revenue; no profit or loss.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Fixed cost** | Does not change with output within installed capacity (e.g. **depreciation**) |
| **Variable cost** | Changes **in proportion** to output (e.g. **raw material**) |
| **Contribution** | **Selling price - variable cost** per unit |
| **BEP (units)** | **Fixed cost / contribution per unit** |
| **BEP (% of capacity)** | BEP units / installed capacity |
| **Margin of safety** | **1 - BEP** (as a share of capacity, at full utilisation) |

**Without unit data:** BEP sales = **fixed cost / (total sales - total variable cost) x total sales** at that capacity level.

**Uses:** BEP fixes the **moratorium** and when **repayment can begin**. **Rule of thumb (courseware):** BEP up to **50 per cent** of capacity is **very healthy**; the higher it is, the riskier; **above 85 per cent is very high risk**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Beyond the break even volume, each extra unit adds its contribution to profit.

self_check.prompt_text: Fixed cost Rs 600, price Rs 20, variable cost Rs 14. What is the BEP in units?

payload.title: Break even and margin of safety
payload.core_explanation_md: A unit has installed capacity of 1,000 units a year, fixed cost of Rs 2,000 a year, variable cost of Rs 7 per unit and a selling price of Rs 12 per unit. Find the contribution, the break even point in units and as a share of capacity, the margin of safety at full capacity and the break even sales value.

worked_steps.description: Contribution per unit.
BEP in units = fixed cost / contribution.
BEP as a share of capacity.
Margin of safety at full capacity.
Break even sales value using revenue figures at full capacity (sales 12,000; variable cost 7,000).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Contribution Rs 5; break even 400 units (40 per cent of capacity); margin of safety 60 per cent; break even sales Rs 4,800

self_check.prompt_text: Check the break even sales value by units.
self_check.expected_takeaway: 400 units x Rs 12 = Rs 4,800, the same.

payload.title: DSCR in project appraisal
payload.core_explanation_md:
**DSCR** fixes the **repayment instalment** in each year so that **servicing is strainless**. The courseware treats a **gross DSCR of 1.50 to 1.75** and a **net DSCR of about 2** as ideal (its own guidance, not a regulatory norm).

| Variant | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| **Net DSCR** | **Cash accrual** / **instalments of term loans due** in the period |
| **Gross DSCR** | **(Cash accrual + interest on term loans)** / **(instalments + interest on term loans)** |

**Average DSCR for the whole repayment period** is **not the arithmetic mean** of yearly ratios. Use the **horizontal sums**:

**Average gross DSCR = (sum of cash accruals + sum of interest) / (sum of instalments + sum of interest)**

For the **average net DSCR**, leave interest out of both.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A bad year (low DSCR) is weighted by its size in the horizontal sums.

self_check.prompt_text: Is the average DSCR the simple mean of the yearly DSCRs?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: it is the ratio of the horizontal sums over all years.

payload.title: Average DSCR over three years
payload.core_explanation_md: For three years, cash accruals are Rs 130, 160 and 190 lakh; interest on term loans is Rs 60, 40 and 20 lakh; and term loan instalments are Rs 80, 100 and 120 lakh. Find the yearly net DSCRs, the average net DSCR and the average gross DSCR, and compare the average gross DSCR with the mean of yearly gross DSCRs.

worked_steps.description: Yearly net DSCR = accrual / instalment.
Average net DSCR = sum of accruals / sum of instalments.
Average gross DSCR = (sum of accruals + sum of interest) / (sum of instalments + sum of interest).
Yearly gross DSCRs and their simple mean.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 1.43 (here equal by coincidence of equal yearly denominators)

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Average net DSCR 1.60; average gross DSCR 1.43; the horizontal-sum method, not the simple mean, is the method to use

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the simple mean differ from the horizontal-sum ratio in general?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because years with larger instalments carry more weight in the horizontal sums.

payload.title: IRR, sensitivity analysis and security cushion ratios
payload.core_explanation_md:
**IRR** is the **discount rate at which the net present value of all future cash flows equals zero**. It is also called the **discounted cash flow rate of return**. The lender watches it to judge whether the **investor will stay interested**, which supports recovery.

**Sensitivity analysis:** projections rest on assumptions, so test the impact on **BEP, DSCR and IRR** if an input or output price turns adverse.

- Normally **four adverse scenarios**, each tested **alone** against the **base case**.
- A **fifth scenario** with **all four adverse together**.
- Go ahead only if BEP, DSCR and IRR stay **acceptable** even then.

**Security cushion**

| Ratio | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| **FACR** | **WDV of fixed assets under charge / term loans outstanding** |
| **SMCR** | **(WDV of fixed assets - term loans outstanding) / WDV x 100** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Compare the base case with the worst case before sanctioning.

self_check.prompt_text: How many adverse scenarios are tested in the combined case?
self_check.expected_takeaway: All four adverse changes at the same time, as a fifth scenario.

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The current official list should be checked for exact inclusion of a sector.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two features of infrastructure projects that make appraisal different.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Long implementation and gestation periods, and a high debt-equity ratio.

payload.title: Financing infrastructure: the 2025 Directions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Finance only** projects that are **technically feasible, financially viable and bankable**, and only if the bank has the **expertise** to appraise them (**risk analysis and sensitivity analysis**).

| Point | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Public sector units** | Term loans only to **corporate entities** (companies or statutory corporations); **not in place of budgetary resources**; **not to fund State budgets** |
| **Servicing** | **Project revenues**, not budget money, must service the debt |
| **SPVs** | For **specific, monitorable projects**; private SPVs must **build infrastructure directly**, **not act as financial intermediaries**; **sponsor's distress must not hurt the SPV** |
| **Forms of finance** | Working capital, **term loan**, **project loan**, **bonds, debentures, preference or equity shares** acquired in the package (**deemed advance**), other funded or non-funded facilities |
| **Government-owned entities** | Do **viability due diligence**; **State Government guarantees are no substitute** for credit appraisal |
| **Appraisal** | **Project risks**, **contract risk mitigation**, **counterparty creditworthiness**; **screening committees or special cells**; consortium banks may use the **lead bank's appraisal** |
| **Prudential** | **Exposure limits**, **risk weights**, **ALM caution** against liquidity mismatch; a **clear approval procedure** and **review of pending applications**; **avoid multiple appraisals** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's promoter equity financing conditions rest on a paragraph that was deleted from 1 July 2026 and are not taught.

self_check.prompt_text: Can a State Government guarantee replace credit appraisal for a government-owned project?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: it is not a substitute for satisfactory credit appraisal.

payload.title: Project finance: phases, sanction and disbursement conditions
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **Project Finance chapter** applies from **1 October 2025**, but not to projects whose **financial closure was achieved by that date**.

**Three phases:** **design** (to financial closure) -> **construction** (financial closure to the day before **actual DCCO**, the date of commencement of commercial operations) -> **operational** (from actual DCCO to full repayment).

**Before disbursement**

- **Financial closure** achieved and **original DCCO documented**.
- **Disbursement schedule** tied to **stage of completion** in the loan agreement.
- **Realistic post-DCCO repayment schedule**; tenor including moratorium **not more than 85 per cent of the project's economic life**.
- **One DCCO** across all lenders.
- **All approvals and clearances** (environmental, legal, regulatory) **before financial closure**.
- **Land or right of way:** **50 per cent** for **PPP infrastructure**, **75 per cent** for all other projects; transmission lines as the bank decides.
- **PPP infrastructure:** disbursement only after the **Appointed Date** is declared.
- Disbursal in step with **completion, equity infusion and other sources**; **lender's independent engineer or architect** certifies stages.

**Minimum exposure of an individual bank in under-construction projects**

| Aggregate exposure of all lenders | Individual bank floor |
| --- | --- |
| Up to **Rs 1,500 crore** | **10 per cent** of aggregate |
| Above **Rs 1,500 crore** | **5 per cent or Rs 150 crore, whichever is higher** |

The floors **end after actual DCCO**. A project loan **can turn NPA before DCCO** on the record of recovery. Keep a **project database**, updated within **15 days** of a change.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Resolution of delayed projects (DCCO deferment) is taught with restructuring in a later unit.

self_check.prompt_text: What land or right of way must be available before disbursement for a non-PPP project?

payload.title: Project finance limits: tenor, exposure floors and land

Find the maximum repayment tenor including moratorium, the minimum land that must be available before disbursement, and the minimum exposure of an individual bank in each case.

payload.title: Partial credit enhancement (PCE) of bonds
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank may give **PCE** to bonds of **corporates and SPVs** for all types of projects, and to bonds of **non-deposit taking NBFCs with assets of Rs 1,000 crore and above** (including HFCs). The aim is to **lift the bond's rating** so the issuer can borrow on **better terms**.

| Feature | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Form** | **Subordinated**, **irrevocable contingent line of credit**, drawn on a **shortfall in cash flows** (may **revolve**); **never a guarantee** |
| **When** | At the **time of the bond issue**; **irrevocable** |
| **Single bank limit** | **50 per cent** of the **bond issue size** |
| **All PCE providers together** | **50 per cent** of the issue size |
| **Rating of the bond** | **Pre-enhanced rating not below BBB minus**, rated by **at least two ECAIs**; reports show **standalone and enhanced** rating |
| **Investing** | The bank **cannot invest** in bonds credit-enhanced by any regulated entity; it may give **other credit** to the issuer |
| **Documents** | A **binding agreement** among **promoter, PCE bank, bondholders (via trustee) and other lenders** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's 20 per cent single-bank limit comes from the 2015 and 2016 circulars and is replaced by 50 per cent.

self_check.prompt_text: May PCE be given as a guarantee?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: it must be an irrevocable contingent line of credit, not a guarantee.

payload.title: Take-out financing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Take-out financing** helps a bank that has made a **long-tenor infrastructure loan** avoid an **asset–liability maturity mismatch**: another financial institution agrees to **take over the outstanding loan** on a **pre-determined basis**.

**RBI position:** a loan transfer should move the **economic interest** with **no change to the loan terms**. If terms are **modified** during or after a transfer (for example in take-out financing), the change is **evaluated against restructuring** under the **Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware describes IDFC and SBI arrangements; these are not taught.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the main purpose of take-out financing?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To avoid asset-liability mismatch from long-tenor infrastructure loans.

payload.title: PCE limits for a bond issue
payload.core_explanation_md: A corporate plans a bond issue of Rs 600 crore. Find the maximum PCE exposure of one bank and of all PCE providers together, and say what the minimum pre-enhanced rating and the minimum number of rating agencies are.

worked_steps.description: A single bank may provide up to 50 per cent of the issue size.
All PCE providers together are also capped at 50 per cent.
Rating and agencies.
worked_steps.formula_or_substitution: pre-enhanced rating not lower than BBB minus; at least two ECAIs

payload.final_answer_with_unit: One bank up to Rs 300 crore; all providers together up to Rs 300 crore; pre-enhanced rating at least BBB minus from at least two ECAIs

self_check.prompt_text: If one bank already provides Rs 300 crore of PCE, how much can another bank add?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nothing, because the aggregate cap of Rs 300 crore is reached.

unresolved: The appraisal method, ratio formulas and descriptions are the courseware's (S01 printed pp. 469 to 480, PDF pp. 484 to 495). The project finance, infrastructure financing and partial credit enhancement rules are taught from RBI/DOR/2025-26/154 (Chapter VII paragraphs 72-87, Chapter IX paragraphs 134-143 and Chapter XVI paragraphs 422-432), not from the courseware, which reproduces older circulars. The copy is the later version (updated October 2026); paragraph 78 and 80 explanations were inserted on 15 July 2026 (after the cut-off) and are not taught; paragraph 137 (promoter equity financing for infrastructure, which the courseware describes) was deleted with effect from 1 July 2026 and its text is not in the copy, so the courseware's promoter equity conditions are NOT taught.

The courseware's account of resolution of project finance accounts with extension of the date of commencement of commercial operations (DCCO deferment of 3 years for infrastructure and 2 years for other projects, cost overrun up to 10 per cent, change in scope up to 25 per cent, 180-day implementation) comes from the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, which was not retrieved; it is NOT taught and is left for the restructuring unit (Module C unit 8).

The courseware's list of infrastructure sectors cites a Gazette notification of 8 April 2016; it is taught only as five broad heads (needs_review) because the harmonised master list has been revised since.

The courseware states the break even point formula with a typographical slip (Rs 200 for Rs 2,000 fixed cost) and an average DSCR formula with a "horizontal sum"; its break even risk bands (up to 50 per cent very healthy, 51 to 65 low risk, 66 to 70 medium, 71 to 85 high, above 85 very high) have a gap between 65 and 66 and are the courseware's rule of thumb, taught without boundary questions. Its IRR formula is not the usual definition; the definition (rate at which net present value is zero) is taught.
The ideal DSCR range (1.50 to 1.75 gross, about 2 net) is the courseware's guidance, not a regulatory norm.

Take-out financing arrangements with IDFC and SBI (courseware pp. 476-477) are not taught; only the concept and the RBI statement that term changes in take-out financing are evaluated against restructuring (RBI_TDCR_2025 paragraph 15) are taught. The courseware's partial credit enhancement limit of 20 per cent for an individual bank (2015 and 2016 circulars) is replaced by the 50 per cent limit in paragraph 426 of the Directions.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
